content: The Global AIDS Monitoring (GAM) indicator emphasizes the importance of disaggregating data for individuals newly initiated on antiretroviral therapy (ART) during the reporting period. This subset of patients is critical for understanding ART retention and outcomes. ART retention is defined as the percentage of people living with HIV who remain on ART 12 months after initiation. It is also recommended to monitor retention at 24, 60 months, and even 10 and 15 years post-initiation. This cohort-based indicator is a vital component of the HIV care cascade, measuring the number of patients who continue treatment over time. ART retention is commonly reported at 12 and 24 months, but with the significant scale-up of ART programs in the past decade, people living with HIV are experiencing improved health and longer survival. Consequently, monitoring retention beyond 12 or 24 months is essential. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends measuring retention at 60 months, 10 years, and 15 years to ensure long-term treatment success. Retention monitoring is prioritized at global, national, subnational, and facility levels, as poor retention in care can lead to treatment interruptions, which are a major barrier to achieving optimal patient and program outcomes, including viral suppression. The denominator for ART retention is defined as the number of patients initiating ART up to 12 months (or 24, 60 months) before the start of the reporting year. This includes patients who have died, stopped ART, or been lost to follow-up (LTFU) by the 12th month (or 24th, 60th month). For example, if the reporting period is January 1 to December 31, 2015, facilities calculate this indicator using all patients who started ART during the 12-month period from January 1 to December 31, 2014. Patients are considered alive and on ART if they have an antiretroviral (ARV) regimen code recorded at 12 months. When ARVs are dispensed for more than one month, a line drawn through the additional months indicates the patient is still receiving care at the facility or another point of care. At the facility level, the numerator excludes patients who are dead, stopped ART, or LTFU at 12 months among those who started ART during the reporting period. However, it includes patients who stopped but restarted ART before month 12 and those transferred in (TI) from another facility. At the national level, patients classified as TI should equal those classified as transferred out (TO) and do not need to be accounted for separately. This simple sum can help validate facility reports. Retention monitoring is particularly important for pregnant and breastfeeding women due to the additional risk of HIV transmission to HIV-exposed infants (HEI). These women require more frequent and earlier retention monitoring than the general population. Retention indicators for pregnant and breastfeeding women focus on follow-up at 1 and 6 months after ART initiation. ART registers should be maintained in all settings where ART is provided, and maternal and child health (MCH)-specific ART registers may facilitate easier data collection. Otherwise, current pregnancy and breastfeeding status should be recorded in the ART follow-up status columns. Retention data can be disaggregated by sex, pregnancy, breastfeeding status, and age groups. Optional disaggregation includes co-infection with tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis B and people who inject drugs. Analyzing LTFU patients is critical, as facility-level LTFU does not necessarily mean patients are not retained in ART programs. LTFU often includes unascertained deaths, self-transferred patients, true LTFU cases, and those alive but not in care or on ART. HIV programs should strive to understand true outcomes among LTFU patients and re-engage those alive and not in care back into treatment. Retention monitoring also highlights the importance of early ART initiation to reduce mortality, particularly among patients presenting with advanced HIV infection. Strengthening early ART initiation can improve survival during the first year of treatment, a period often associated with higher mortality due to delayed treatment initiation. Viral load suppression is another critical indicator, measuring the percentage of people living with HIV on ART who achieve virological suppression. This cross-sectional indicator can be calculated using either a population-based denominator (for settings with ≥75% viral load testing coverage) or a program-based denominator (for settings with <75% testing coverage). Results should be interpreted cautiously, accounting for missing data and other limitations.
